chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from the one who mentioned it, from Al-Walid ibn Abi al-A'ala, from Mu'tab, who said:

Muhammad ibn Bishr al-Washa' came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and asked him to speak to Shihab so that he would lighten the burden on him until the season (of Hajj) expired. There was a debt of one thousand dinars owed to him by Muhammad. So he (the Imam) sent for him, and he came to him. The Imam said to him: 'You know the state of Muhammad and his cutting off from people to be with us, and he has mentioned that you have a thousand dinars owed to you by him, which have not gone into a belly or a private part (marriage), but have gone as a debt on men and expenses he incurred. And I would love for you to make him free from it.'

Shihab said: 'Perhaps you are from those who claim that good deeds are taken from him and given to me.' He said: 'That is so in our hands (the narrations).' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah is more Generous and more Just than that His servant comes close to Him, stands in the clear night (in prayer), or fasts in the hot day, or circumambulates this House, and then He strips him of that and gives it to you. But Allah has abundant bounty that suffices the believer.' So Shihab said: 'Then he is free (from my debt).'

key_terms.أَلْفُ دِينَارٍ: One thousand dinars (a significant sum of gold currency)
key_terms.اللَّهُ أَكْرَمُ وَ أَعْدَلُ: Allah is more Generous and more Just
key_terms.لَمْ تَذْهَبْ فِي بَطْنٍ وَ لَا فَرْجٍ: Has not gone into a belly or a private part (indicating the money was spent on living expenses and debts, not consumed or married away)
key_terms.يُقْبَضُ مِنْ حَسَنَاتِهِ: That his good deeds are taken/captured

ai.seo_question: How does the Imam justify the forgiveness of debt without deducting from the debtor's good deeds?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *al-afw* (exemption) where a creditor forgives a debtor's debt not through material payment, but by accepting the debtor's spiritual merits (*hasanat*). Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that Allah’s justice ensures a believer’s worship is not merely 'transferred' or stripped away to settle a debt, but rather, divine bounty compensates the believer, rendering the debt void. This narrative underscores the theological balance between divine generosity (*fadl*) and justice (*adl*), affirming that spiritual acts retain their value even when used to settle worldly obligations.
